By Charlotte Goldstone
6 October 2026
South Korean logistics group LX Pantos has completed a $167m logistics centre in Katowice, Poland, as it expands its footprint in Central and Eastern Europe.
The 109,000 sq metre complex of five buildings was jointly acquired by LX Pantos, the Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corp, and PIS No 2 Fund, the latter under South Korea’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, with financing provided in part by Korea Ocean Business Corp.
LX Pantos said the facility in Upper Silesia would become a strategic hub for its Eastern European operations, supporting customers in sectors including automotive, consumer goods, and home appliances. It also expects the site to support other Korean companies expanding into Europe.
Katowice sits at the intersection of major east-west and north-south transport corridors, with road, rail, and air connections linking Germany, Poland, Ukraine, and northern and southern Europe.
The investment comes amid a trend of manufacturers and supply chains shifting towards Central and Eastern Europe. Paweł Kaźmierczak, chief commercial officer of 4R Cargo, told The Loadstar, on the sidelines of Aviation Connect last week, Poland and the wider region had been developing rapidly for several years, citing labour availability and skills, and economic growth as key factors.
He pointed to companies also having adopted a “China plus one” strategy following Covid, moving some production into Eastern Europe. The war in Ukraine and subsequent sanctions had accelerated some relocations, he added, including aircraft-parts manufacturing moving to Poland and Slovakia.
“We are riding the wave of economic growth,” said Mr Kaźmierczak. “We were in the right place at the right time, and we took advantage of that.”
For logistics providers, industrial expansion is creating demand beyond ecommerce, with Mr Kaźmierczak highlighting pharmaceuticals, aircraft parts, and automotive manufacturing as important cargo flows in the region.
Poland’s role as a logistics gateway is also being shaped by the war in Ukraine.

By Alex Lennane
6 October 2026
Canada’s efforts to reduce its reliance on the US are opening new opportunities for transatlantic air cargo, but forwarders warn that limited capacity and seasonal reductions in passenger flights could complicate the shift.
Edmonton International Airport said its EU-bound cargo increased in 2025 while exports to the US fell, and expects record European flows this year.
Alex Lowe, director, ecommerce, cargo, and aviation real estate, explained: “So far the data trend suggests 2026 will be a record year for air cargo from YEG to the EU.”
The airport also expects record EU imports this year, with turbine parts, medical diagnostic equipment, and specialised machinery among its leading inbound commodities.
Mr Lowe said trade diversification could encourage greater use of airfreight as Canadian businesses developed relationships with more distant markets.
“From an air cargo perspective, we welcome this trend as it encourages trade with markets that may lean towards increased air cargo, given the geographic distances.”
However, turning that opportunity into sustained business will require sufficient capacity.
“Both our passenger and cargo data does show that the YEG market is underserved to/from the EU, so we are working with existing airline partners and potential new entrants to develop increased transatlantic air services, and/or increased capacity,” he said. “The ability to offer consistent two-way cargo volumes is a strong contributor to our business case.”
Steffen Manz, CEO of Speed Global Logistics, said the challenge extended beyond Edmonton.
“Capacity remains a significant bottleneck, particularly for Western Canada, meaning a substantial portion of western cargo must still route through eastern gateways or US hubs.”
He said West Canadian shippers depended on seasonal passenger belly capacity and domestic feeder networks connecting with eastern gateways.
But diversification is already generating new airfreight business, according to Mr Manz, who cited an Ontario-based automotive and electronics manufacturer that had previously sent component sub-assemblies by truck to a customer in the US Midwest.
Following the introduction of tariffs, he said, the Canadian supplier became uncompetitive on that lane and activated a backup supply agreement with a German automotive systems integrator.
“Because the new supply chain had to be stood up immediately, to prevent factory downtime, the initial months of volume shifted entirely from domestic trucking to expedited transatlantic airfreight to Frankfurt and Liège, generating entirely new lane demand for the air cargo network.”
Official figures support the broader change in trading patterns, although they also underline the importance of distinguishing trade value from freight volumes.
Statistics Canada reports that merchandise exports to non-US countries rose 17.2% in value in 2025, while exports to the US fell 5.8%. Total merchandise trade with non-US countries increased 14.3%.
Gold was an important contributor: exports of unwrought gold, silver, and platinum-group metals and their alloys – predominantly gold – rose 41.7% in value amid rising prices. Excluding that category, total Canadian merchandise exports fell 3%.
Transport Canada’s 2025 annual report also identified weaker cross-border trucking and rail activity alongside increased overseas shipments and air cargo. It noted 8% more air cargo with Europe, mainly gold and aircraft.
The Canadian International Freight Forwarders Association (CIFFA) said businesses were exploring alternatives to US suppliers, reflecting changing consumer preferences as well as tariffs.
It said some additional freight was moving between Canada and Europe, but warned that the transition into winter airline schedules would reduce available widebody services.
However, Canada’s Cargojet has added capacity, launching a Wednesday 767 freighter service on 23 September, between Hamilton, Halifax, and Liège, returning to Hamilton. The service complements its weekend operation and connects with its Canadian overnight network.
CIFFA suggested the additional flight could absorb some of the capacity lost as passenger airlines reduce their European services.
CIFFA also cautioned that Edmonton’s growth could partly reflect the additional European airline services over the summer, rather than solely a change in shippers’ trading relationships.
The economics of diversification remain challenging. CIFFA highlighted the difficulty of moving bulky or heavy goods by air, while higher fuel costs could make alternative routings prohibitively expensive. Airfreight was better suited to higher-value finished goods, it added.
Mr Manz, nevertheless, believes the change will endure. He said: “Evidence points to this being a sustained, structural shift rather than a temporary trend.”
Export Development Canada’s 2026 Trade Confidence Index found 31% of Canadian exporters planned to enter Europe in the next two years. EDC is also expanding its European presence with new representations in France and Sweden, and another planned for Poland in 2027.
Meanwhile, Edmonton sees pharmaceuticals as a further source of potential demand. Applied Pharmaceutical Innovation is developing a Critical Medicines Production Centre in the region, with capacity to produce 70 million doses annually. The airport said operations were expected to begin later this year or in early 2027.
“Air cargo is a critical contributor to revenue on our passenger flights to the EU as belly cargo,” it said. “Our team is always working to find and grow the cargo contributions for our airline partners.”
The airport is also developing its International Cargo Hub, which it said was budgeted at more than C$350m (US$245m). Work includes expanded freighter aprons, a fuel hydrant system, additional perishables and pharmaceutical handling facilities, and infrastructure to serve a 2,000-acre cargo and logistics park.
“These investments align perfectly with the Canadian government’s objectives to diversify Canada’s trade profile internationally and open up global markets for western Canadian businesses.”

ZF Commercial Vehicle Solutions raised its U.S. sales outlook for next year by about $50 million, an executive said at a media briefing ahead of IAA Transportation in Hanover, Germany. The German supplier also paused a U.S. hybridization project with a lead customer and is concentrating its new TraXon Hybrid transmission on Europe and Japan.
Fabian Schlegel, global head of sales and head of the EMEA region at ZF CVS, said he and Dirk Wohltmann, head of ZF CVS in North America, made the decision in a meeting with executive management in Switzerland the week before the briefing.
“What gives me confidence: trucks and trailers aged brutally over the last years because everyone was cautious on replacement,” Schlegel said. “Mileage is there; trucks are not standing still. You come into the need to replace. Not a bonanza, but a nice increase.”
ZF had planned for a flat U.S. market this year. Demand has climbed sharply since the second quarter, Schlegel said, and ZF plants pulled in up to two months of production ahead of schedule to keep customers supplied.
U.S. demand runs ahead of plan
ZF’s North American business grew 23.7% last year to $1.32 billion in revenue, said Wohltmann, who is based in Auburn Hills, Mich., and also leads R&D for the Americas.
“Good trend upward,” he said of the U.S. market. “Freight is demanding. Fleets starting to update equipment. Uncertainty is the word of the year. Not a tremendous exploding market — a healthy, forward-looking one.”
Asked about tariffs and diesel prices, Wohltmann said, “Challenging, but the market held for a while and now it’s at the point of invest. High diesel even fuels the drive for efficient solutions.”
Wohltmann pointed to ZF’s PowerLine eight-speed automatic, built at its plant in Gray Court, S.C., which is available with Paccar and coming soon to Daimler Truck North America. The company is also pitching an electric trailer built around its AxTrax driven axle, which uses regenerative braking to charge batteries, run a reefer unit, and help push the combination. Fuel savings depend on the use case, he said, and go “way above 10%,” with the best case getting close to 20%.
New business and cash flow
ZF CVS has booked more than €5 billion ($5.7 billion) in lifetime business so far in 2026, according to ZF’s Sept. 15 IAA press release . Schlegel put the division’s win rate in customer acquisitions at more than 90% and described the strategy as profitability over scale.
“We don’t take business at a bad margin ,” he said.
Across the group, adjusted free cash flow more than doubled to €989 million ($1.13 billion) in the first half, from €465 million ($530 million) a year earlier, according to ZF’s July 30 half-year results . Schlegel said stronger cash generation let ZF pay back a first tranche of debt in the first half, ahead of its second-half plan.
Hybrid focus shifts to Europe and Japan
TraXon Hybrid was ZF’s lead pitch at IAA. It is built on the TraXon 2 automated manual transmission and reuses parts from ZF’s electrified drivetrain platform. ZF has sold more than 1.5 million TraXon transmissions, all in the heavy class, Schlegel said.
“Leaving politics aside: we had a lead customer in the U.S. very interested,” Schlegel said. “Given the current frame, the U.S. hybridization project is for the moment paused.”
Europe and Japan are the current focus, he said, and ZF is “on the way to sign first customer contracts” for the hybrid. Five days after the briefing, TraXon Hybrid won the Truck Innovation Award 2027 from the International Truck of the Year jury at IAA Transportation, Automotive World reported .
For the U.S., Wohltmann said an electric trailer pulled by a diesel tractor “is already an entry to a hybrid setup.”
“If we can show TCO improvement and ROI around year two, it will get interest in the U.S.,” he said.

By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
6 October 2026
As its emerging economy pursues maritime-driven growth, India appears willing to simplify the regulatory system for foreign-flag containerships operating out of the country.
Reflecting a more liberalised approach, the Indian authorities have scrapped a licensing requirement for vessels chartered by foreign lines through local entities registered in the new business district in Gujarat State better known as “GIFT City”.
Business units operating on the financial centre have multiple regulatory advantages – more particularly, significant tax exemptions – and several mainline and shortsea container lines reportedly already have presence at GIFT City, including CMA CGM, Maersk, and Unifeeder.
And, acting on that strength, several container line heavyweights have implemented vessel reflagging in India – six changes by CMA CGM and twoby Maersk.
The French shipping giant remains particularly upbeat on India. While reflagging one vessel the Marseille-based carrier said: “With India playing an increasingly important role in the global trade, CMA CGM remains dedicated to supporting the country’s maritime ecosystem and contributing to its economic development through strategic initiatives and enhanced service offerings.
“India represents a strategic market for the CMA CGM group,” it added.
MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have promised to follow suit in local tonnage development, according to sources.
The move to abolish a licensing requirement that involved considerable documentation for each call seeking to enter Indian waters is a significant policy relaxation, aimed at pushing the “ease-of-doing-business environment” for investors. And industry sources claimed it would allow “greater operational flexibility” for carriers.
The exemption also builds on other policy reconfigurations. New Delhi recently agreed to continue with the cabotage law waiver for foreign vessels, after moving to revoke the 2018 policy reform earlier this year. The liberal regime permits foreign lines to move transhipment cargo and empty boxes between Indian ports without restrictions, a great enabler in the context of ever-increasing trade volatility.
However, despite the cabotage rule modification, Indian coastal trades remain the domain of vessels registered locally.

When NFL linebacker Micah Parsons was traded from Dallas to Green Bay in 2025, Fanatics had 175,000 jerseys sitting in warehouses with his name on the back and the Cowboys’ branding. The trade suddenly made that inventory worth much less, according to Ben Pivar , SVP and Head of Brands and Supply Chain Technology at Fanatics.
What’s Related
“This wasn’t the reason, but it might have been a catalyst to say, hey, we really need to change,” Pivar said at o9 Solutions’ aim10x Americas event in Chicago.
Fanatics plans to add another production option between ordering finished merchandise months ahead and printing products when demand spikes. Suppliers would hold blank shirts and jerseys that could be customized later, giving Fanatics more time before committing inventory to a particular player.
Pivar projected $15 million in savings from the planned approach, plus $65 million in cost reductions through inventory management. These are expected benefits, not savings already achieved.
RELATED STORIES: How the Savannah Bananas Built a Traveling Retail Supply Chain | Six Things to Consider Before Buying Planning Software
Three approaches to production
Fanatics has traditionally used two approaches. One relies on overseas production with long lead times, requiring decisions about finished merchandise months before it knows how a season will unfold. It offers lower costs, but a player trade or injury can reduce demand for merchandise the company has already produced.
The other uses domestic printing for custom orders and sudden demand around events such as the Super Bowl or playoffs. Products are printed as demand develops.
The planned middle option would use suppliers in nearby countries and the United States to hold blank apparel, with printing happening later.
“They’re going to own the inventory on our behalf,” Pivar said. “We are going to print on demand.”
Pivar described a risk-based approach to choosing among the three production options, with traditional overseas production offering the lowest cost.
Blank inventory brings its own costs
Holding blanks delays the commitment to a player’s name, but managing them still requires planning. Pivar described figuring out how to manage blank inventory as “a pretty major investment” and noted that team colors also have to be considered.
Suppliers therefore need forecasts for which unfinished products to hold and where. Delaying printing will not help fill an order if the right blank jersey is unavailable.
Pivar said the next planning project would include gathering supplier production information to help Fanatics decide where to place orders.
Multiple factories can make the same product, but their locations affect tariffs , inbound costs, and total costs to deliver merchandise. The next phase is intended to help Fanatics weigh those differences when placing orders.
Start with the demand forecast
Fanatics was using o9 for demand planning when Pivar spoke in September and had purchased the software for its next phase. He expected that inventory and supply planning work, covering both finished merchandise and blanks, to begin by the end of 2026.
Fanatics started with a 24-month rolling forecast and a process for its wholesale and e-commerce teams to agree on expected demand, with warehouse and transportation teams also needing visibility into the plan. Once that process was stable, it added AI and machine learning to help improve forecasting.
Pivar reported a $20 million inventory reduction from the demand planning project to date. That result is separate from the projected benefits of the three-part production strategy.
Delaying customization still requires a demand forecast. Fanatics uses that forecast to guide inventory and sourcing decisions.
“The forecast is the foundation for this,” Pivar said.

Volvo Autonomous Solutions and Waabi announced Monday they are hauling freight for Warp, the first customer operation in the companies’ partnership. Volvo VNL Autonomous trucks running the Waabi Driver are moving Warp freight directly to third-party facilities on the Dallas-Houston corridor, with an observer in the driver’s seat.
Warp runs less-than-truckload and full-truckload freight through a single network and lists Walmart, DoorDash, and Gopuff among its customers. CEO Daniel Sokolovsky founded AxleHire before Warp emerged from stealth in 2022 .
“Warp is a fantastic example where we can demonstrate the value of driving next-level efficiency for LTL consolidation, and remind people that hours-of-service benefits do not necessarily need to translate into a coast-to-coast, team-driving unlock,” said Lior Ron, COO of Waabi, in an interview with FreightWaves. “They can also help drive efficiency on a Dallas-Houston corridor, and continuous consolidation and efficiency of the LTL network.”
LTL linehaul often runs slip-seat, with one driver taking a tractor for a shift and the next driver picking it up after. Federal rules cap each driver at 11 hours behind the wheel after 10 consecutive hours off duty .
“Imagine a future where you can run those networks and consolidate on a continuous basis without hours of service , and just drive efficiency and utilization,” Ron said.
Ron said scheduling and balancing those networks gets harder “with what’s happening in the market now, between capacity exiting the market and fuel.” He said demand for autonomy has grown since he last spoke with FreightWaves.
“The value of autonomy grows when you can coordinate the freight around it,” Sokolovsky said in the announcement. “Warp brings together shipments from multiple customers and aligns routes, capacity, and timing, so advances on a single lane can benefit the broader network.”
Driverless Waits on Volvo’s Purpose-Built Truck
Waabi trained its software on a Peterbilt 579 test fleet and moved it to the Volvo VNL Autonomous without retraining this summer. The Volvo truck carries redundancies for six safety-critical systems, according to the announcement.
Ron said Waabi believes a driverless truck should come from an OEM’s factory, fully redundant and validated by the manufacturer.
“Although we are ready, we are choosing not to retrofit our way into driverless, and to wait until Volvo is ready,” Ron said. “The good news is Volvo is on track. You see their public commitments, and we are fully on track for driverless next year, with Volvo as the first OEM platform.”
Volvo expects to begin installing Waabi’s system in the first quarter of 2027, Forbes reported last month.
Opening Lanes Without Retraining
Last month, Waabi’s truck ran the Dallas-San Antonio lane for the first time with zero disengagements. Ron said Waabi maps a new lane with a single truck pass, building a light map the system treats as another safety sensor. The truck gets no autonomy training on the lane, he said.
Waabi has cut the time to open a lane from three months to three weeks, and with San Antonio, to none, Ron said.
“What changes is the ask,” Ron said. Waabi no longer has to ask a shipper whether it has loads moving from Dallas to Houston. It can ask where the shipper’s most acute pain point is, the same conversation Ron said he had with customers at Uber Freight, which he founded and ran as CEO .
“Let’s solve those pain points with autonomy now, versus waiting for autonomy to catch up,” he said.
During a keynote at a supply chain executive conference in Las Vegas last month, Ron asked the audience who had ridden in a Waymo. About three-quarters raised a hand. About half raised a hand when he asked who wants to deploy autonomy in their network in the next three years.
“We’re on track, and we’re seeing massive customer demand,” Ron said. “It’s crazy, because we’re beyond the early adopters now.”

source_document.body:
While AI is taking off in biopharma for administrative tasks and drug discovery efforts, more than 90% of drugmakers have yet to commit to scaling AI use in regulated biopharma manufacturing, according to CRB’s new Horizons: Life Sciences report.
Fewer than 10% of drugmakers are scaling AI to support clinical or commercial manufacturing, a survey of more than 400 R&D and manufacturing professionals found .
CRB, a company that designs and builds biopharma facilities, ran the survey for its 2026 Horizons report on the investment choices of life sciences companies. The survey found widespread use of AI in nonregulated areas, with 56% of respondents applying the technology to administrative workflows and 45% using it in drug discovery. Yet uptake in regulated manufacturing is lower.
Asked about their use of AI in clinical or commercial manufacturing, just 1% of respondents said that they are currently using the technology in most or all applications, while 8% are scaling AI for use in many regulated manufacturing applications and 17% are scaling the tech for a few applications.
The remaining 74% of respondents could be several years away, at best, from applying AI to regulated medicine production.

CRB linked the figures to concerns about the suitability of current AI models for regulated manufacturing environments. Almost half of respondents named accuracy or quality concerns as major issues for the use of AI in clinical or commercial manufacturing. Insufficient validation standards were the next most commonly cited issues, followed by unclear accountability and a lack of transparency and explainability.
Respondents did appear to see an AI-based future. CRB found that 31% of those surveyed, including 24% of people who have yet to secure funding for AI adoption, plan to use the technology in the next three years. Another 31% of respondents are considering using AI in drug production but are yet to adopt a formal plan for the rollout. Just 12% of respondents have no plans to use AI in regulated manufacturing.
The findings echo comments by manufacturing leaders, who have noted the challenge of providing the interpretable outputs expected by agencies when using models with internal workings that are a mystery to users. Experts have also reported data integrity and traceability issues linked to the need for models to be version-controlled, audit-trailed and compliant with FDA regulations governing electronic records.
Indeed, AI use triggered a warning letter from the agency in April. FDA inspectors found Purolea Cosmetics Lab’s use of AI to create drug product specifications, procedures and master production or control records violated rules on the responsibilities of quality control units. The FDA told Purolea that “any output or recommendations from an AI agent must be reviewed and cleared by an authorized human representative.”

source_document.body:
By Alexander Whiteman
6 October 2026
Strong volume growth along the West African coast growth is proving the double-edged sword some had warned of, with many of the ports that had been reaping rewards now subject to heavy and intensifying congestion.
Ghana, Guinea, and Sierra Leone are among the countries most affected by delays sprouting up along the coast, all three rapidly approaching similar volumes to those handled in the entirety of 2025.
Forwarders active on West African trades told The Loadstar they too had observed the congestion hobbling many of the ports’ ability to function effectively, one expressing concern over looming temperature-controlled cargo due for delivery.
A forwarder with volumes destined for Temam in Ghanam told The Loadstar : “CMA CGM has announced a congestion charge of $400 per teu for these shipments. This means an additional cost of $800 for each 40ft refrigerated container.”
Hapag-Lloyd has also announced a $250 surcharge on reefer shipments destined for Tema, which became applicable for shipments sailing as of yesterday, adding to the worries of cargo owners.
The carrier has warned customers to expect delays of 10 days for discharging and loading goods, although Portcast claims that the situation at the Ghanian port may be improving, average waits having fallen below the four-day average, an improvement on last week.
Instead, it singles Conakry and Freetown as the ports to be concerned about, congestion delays at both exceeding 10 days – a rapid deterioration at the Sierra Leone capital’s gateway saw delays increase by four days, week on week, and by more than a day at Conakry.
Only a month ago, Sierra Leone Ports and Harbours Authority director general Yankuba Askia Bio claimed a “decongestion” effort, led by multiple stakeholders, had succeeded, resulting in Freetown being removed from a list of congested African gateways.
Efforts at Conakry to mitigate the worst of the congestion have seen trucks operating around the clock at Guinea’s main gateway to keep cargo flowing, and ensure the backlog does not worsen. While at Tema, the Ghana Shippers’ Authority said last month it was working with the port authority, shipping lines, and terminal operators to increase vessel calls to accelerate empty-container evacuation.
But there is growing recognition across the sector that against a backdrop of surging volume growth, the ports are delaying what will inevitably be needed if they are to avoid a catastrophic collapse in supply chains – investment and expansion in infrastructure.

source_document.body:
There are plenty of ways to build a small electric vehicle. These days, the prevailing options have been to make it faster, give it more power, slap on bigger tires, or keep adding features until your humble little scooter has somehow turned into a 150-pound electric motorcycle.
Or you can be brave and go in the other direction to ask a simpler question: How much vehicle do people actually need for all those short trips around town?
That’s essentially the idea behind the Lightfoot, a wonderfully weird new solar-powered electric scooter from San Francisco R&D company Otherlab. The two-seat electric scooter tops out at just under 20 mph (32 km/h), carries a surprisingly large amount of cargo, and covers both sides of its body in solar panels capable of adding up to 18 miles (29 km) of range per day.
And as someone who has long argued that we need more small electric vehicles – not simply faster and heavier e-bikes and e-mopeds – I’m pretty intrigued.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The Lightfoot has actually been kicking around for a while, and I covered the prototype’s unveiling nearly two years ago. But now it’s finally available for sale and delivery. The first 100 Launch Edition scooters are priced at $4,495 including delivery , with a refundable $100 reservation required to get in line. Those initial scooters will be available in sky blue and solar orange. A bit on the nose, but I like it.
Sure, $4.5k certainly isn’t cheap for a 20 mph electric scooter.
But then again, there aren’t many other electric scooters that can recharge themselves while you’re buying groceries, or fit 45 liters (1.6 cubic feet) of those groceries inside their body panels on the ride home instead of wearing a hiking backpack full of grains and veggies.
Yes, those solar panels actually do something
The most visually obvious feature of the Lightfoot is the pair of 120W solar panels built directly into the sides of the scooter.
Together, the 240W system can add a claimed 3-4 miles (5-6 km) of range per hour in good sunlight, or as much as 18 miles (29 km) over the course of a day.
That’s actually a meaningful amount of solar charging for this type of vehicle.
The trick is that Lightfoot doesn’t require much energy in the first place. Its 52V and 1,560Wh battery is rated for up to 37 miles (60 km) of range. That means someone commuting 5 miles (8 km) each way and leaving the scooter parked outside all day could theoretically replenish most or even all of their daily energy from sunlight under favorable conditions.
Of course, let’s keep the solar thing in perspective. A 1.5 kWh battery isn’t exactly an electric Hummer battery pack. Lightfoot includes a 230W onboard charger and can be plugged into a normal wall outlet, with a full charge taking around four hours. So that means sunshine isn’t necessary to make the scooter practical; it simply gives owners another option.
But there’s something undeniably cool about owning a vehicle that you might rarely need to plug in if your daily trips are short enough.
Sure, there may be downsides. It looks like a strong crosswind could have you tacking back and forth across the lane like a sailboat, and I’m sure they’ve got a solution for locking up – but I can’t quite imagine what it would be with no exposed frame members. But hey, it looks like an engineer’s dream – and I’m an engineer.
More than just a solar science experiment
Fortunately, Lightfoot seems to have put some thought into the rest of the scooter, too.
Power comes from a pair of 750W nominal geared hub motors – one in each wheel – rated at 1,000W peak each. Lightfoot claims a whopping 160 Nm of combined torque, meaning most hills shouldn’t be a problem.
The important takeaway though is that this isn’t supposed to be a high-speed machine. All that motor is there to haul people and cargo up those hills while keeping the speed below 20 mph (32 km/h). Again, they’re pitching this as a bike lane solution, not an electric motorcycle.
There’s also full suspension, with a 70mm-travel inverted front fork and a 45mm-travel rear coil-over shock. Tektro hydraulic disc brakes with 160mm rotors provide stopping power, while chunky 14 x 3.2-inch tires should help soak up rough pavement.
And despite its scooter-sized footprint, this isn’t exactly a featherweight. The lightfoot weighs 141 lb (64 kg) and has a 48-inch wheelbase.
Some of that heft buys you a feature I really like, such as that 45 liter (1.5 cubic foot) lockable, weatherproof cargo compartment inside the body. Lightfoot says that’s enough for three grocery bags.
Even better, there’s room for a passenger. The long bench seat is designed for two riders, meaning this isn’t merely a funky commuter. It can handle a grocery run and then pick someone up on the way home without forcing you to choose between your passenger and your pasta.
Though I will say that the thin PU seat cushion looks roughly as plush as an extra-absorbent maxi pad. Perhaps it’s more comfortable than it looks. I’d certainly be fascinated to find out.
Lighting includes a 2,000-lumen headlight, accelerometer-activated taillight, and a rather serious 120 dB horn. There’s also a lockable center stand, Bluetooth-enabled display, and regenerative braking.
What about those bike lanes?
This is where things become slightly more complicated.
Otherlab pitches Lightfoot as a vehicle for both city streets and bike lanes and says it doesn’t require a license or registration.
But micromobility regulations vary significantly by state and municipality, so riders should check their local laws rather than assuming a sub-20 mph (32 km/h) top speed automatically makes Lightfoot legal everywhere a bicycle can go.
Conceptually, though, that’s clearly the territory Lightfoot is aiming for. This isn’t a 50 mph (80 km/h) Sur-Ron competitor masquerading as an e-bike. It’s a sub-20 mph seated scooter intended for the same sort of short urban trips already being made on electric kick scooters and other low-speed micromobility vehicles.
So as long as there aren’t some disqualifiers like the lack of pedals, it should be fairly easy to fit into the expanding definitions of micromobility vehicles in most places.
Electrek’s Take
I love this idea.
Not necessarily because I think everyone needs solar panels hanging off the sides of their scooter, but because I think we desperately need more experimentation in the space between an e-bike and a car.
There are millions of trips where a 4,500 lb (2,000 kg) automobile is ridiculous overkill, yet people still want weather-protected storage, the ability to carry a passenger, enough torque for hills, and something they can simply hop on and ride.
Lightfoot checks a surprising number of those boxes.
It’s admittedly expensive. At $4,495 , you’re paying significantly more than many 20 mph (32 km/h) seated electric scooters, including machines like the Infinite Machine Olto. And unlike the Olto, which can be unlocked to around 36 mph (55 km/h), Lightfoot isn’t secretly offering you a faster vehicle underneath its low-speed settings. At least, not that I know of.
But speed isn’t really the point here.
You’re paying for the unusual design, the big enclosed cargo compartment, two-person capability, full suspension, dual motors, and – obviously – those giant solar panels.
If all you need is something with two wheels that travels 20 mph, I don’t think Lightfoot makes much financial sense. There are much cheaper ways to accomplish that.
But if your daily mileage is low enough that you could genuinely run largely on sunshine, you’ve got somewhere outdoors to park it, and you want a highly practical little vehicle that looks like absolutely nothing else on the road, then I can see the appeal.
The bigger question is whether enough people are willing to pay a premium for that appeal. Otherlab has built an interesting answer to the question of what a short-trip, self-sustaining vehicle could look like. Now we’ll get to find out whether there are enough buyers asking the same question.

source_document.body:
For most Americans, electricity is so woven into daily life that we rarely consider what its absence means. Hospitals depend on it to preserve medicines and operate equipment. Schools, factories, farms, and businesses depend on it to function. Reliable electricity is one of the foundations of a modern economy.
COMMENTARY
Yet 655 million people worldwide still live without access to electricity, according to the latest global assessment released in 2026. And those figures do not fully capture communities where electricity is unreliable, unaffordable, or insufficient to support industrial development and sustained economic growth.
At the same time, global electricity demand is accelerating. The International Energy Agency projects demand to grow by an average of 3.6% annually through 2030, with emerging and developing economies accounting for nearly 80% of the increase. Industry, air conditioning, transportation, and data centers are all adding to the need for power.
Countries facing that growth will not wait indefinitely. They will look for partners that can help them build the energy systems they need.
Small modular reactors (SMRs) could become an important part of that equation.
SMRs are smaller nuclear reactors that can be better suited to countries with smaller electricity systems and can allow utilities to add generating capacity incrementally as demand grows.
Their promise goes beyond size. Greater standardization and modular construction could reduce some of the barriers that have historically limited nuclear power to the largest electricity systems and economies.
But an SMR is unlike other generating equipment.
A country cannot responsibly purchase a reactor and build the institutions around it afterward. Nuclear power requires an effective regulator, appropriate laws, trained operators, and engineers, safeguards, physical security, emergency planning, suitable sites, fuel arrangements, waste management, and a financing framework capable of supporting a project for decades.
For countries considering nuclear power for the first time, developing these institutions can be as consequential as selecting the reactor itself.
That is why the State Department’s Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology program, known as FIRST, deserves strong American support.
FIRST helps partner countries develop the institutional foundation necessary to pursue nuclear energy under high standards of safety, security, and nonproliferation. It begins years before the sale of a reactor, when governments are determining whether nuclear power makes sense, what technologies fit their grids, how projects might be financed, and what laws, regulations, and technical capabilities they must put in place.
Many countries interested in nuclear energy today are years away from being ready to purchase an American reactor. That does not mean the U.S. can afford to wait until they are ready.
Nuclear relationships are built long before procurement begins. Regulatory frameworks are established. Engineers are trained. Sites are evaluated. Financing relationships develop. Technical standards, fuel strategies, and licensing philosophies take shape.
If the U.S. is absent during those formative years, other countries will not wait for us. Russia and China actively offer nuclear technology together with financing, training, and long-term government-to-government relationships. Countries seeking nuclear power may enter those ecosystems years before they are ready to build a reactor.
Once they do, changing course becomes far more difficult.
The pathway a country follows in developing its nuclear program has consequences for safety, security, transparency, and nonproliferation. Countries that work with the U.S. from the beginning are exposed to a licensing and regulatory culture built around independent oversight, rigorous safety requirements, safeguards, and transparent institutions.
Engaging countries early therefore gives the U.S. an opportunity to shape not only which technologies ultimately compete, but how nuclear programs themselves are developed.
Strong safeguards, independent regulation, transparent procurement, and rigorous safety standards reduce risk. They give governments greater confidence in their nuclear programs and provide responsible companies, lenders, and investors with a stronger foundation on which to participate. FIRST places those principles at the beginning of the decision-making process rather than treating them as requirements to be addressed later.
The U.S. has deep capabilities across the nuclear sector. But American companies cannot expect to compete successfully if they enter a market only when a government is ready to sign a reactor contract.
By then, some of the most consequential choices may already have been made. Regulatory requirements may reflect another country’s technology. Engineering work may have been designed around another supplier. Workforce training, financing arrangements, and fuel strategies may already point toward a particular nuclear ecosystem.
Programs such as FIRST allow the U.S. to engage countries while those decisions are still being made. They help governments build the capacity to evaluate competing technologies and financing arrangements while creating a pathway from initial interest to feasibility, engineering, financing, and ultimately investment.
At the United States Energy Association (USEA) , we have spent decades bringing American energy expertise together with governments and utilities around the world. We have seen that durable energy partnerships are built long before equipment is purchased. They begin with technical cooperation, trusted institutions, and relationships among the people who will ultimately plan, finance, regulate, build, and operate energy infrastructure.
A reactor may operate for 60 years or more, and during that time countries may depend on outside partners for fuel, components, engineering expertise, software, maintenance, and other services. Choosing a nuclear technology can therefore mean choosing a network of strategic, commercial, and technical relationships that lasts for generations.
For the U.S., helping countries build secure and responsible nuclear programs advances several interests at once. It promotes high standards of safety and nonproliferation. It creates opportunities for American technology and expertise. And it gives those governments an alternative to nuclear development models offered by Russia and China.
The world needs considerably more electricity. Hundreds of millions of people still have none, while emerging economies are preparing for unprecedented growth in demand.
Those countries will find partners to help them meet it.
The strategic question for the U.S. is whether we begin building those partnerships while countries are still deciding what their nuclear future will look like—or arrive after those decisions have already been made.
With advanced nuclear technology, an extraordinary private sector, and programs such as FIRST, the U.S. has the opportunity to engage early.
We should take it.

Nuclear relationships are built long before procurement begins. Regulatory frameworks are established. Engineers are trained. Sites are evaluated. Financing relationships develop. Technical standards, fuel strategies, and licensing philosophies take shape.

The pathway a country follows in developing its nuclear program has consequences for safety, security, transparency, and nonproliferation. Countries that work with the U.S. from the beginning are exposed to a licensing and regulatory culture built around independent oversight, rigorous safety requirements, safeguards, and transparent institutions.

Strong safeguards, independent regulation, transparent procurement, and rigorous safety standards reduce risk. They give governments greater confidence in their nuclear programs and provide responsible companies, lenders, and investors with a stronger foundation on which to participate. FIRST places those principles at the beginning of the decision-making process rather than treating them as requirements to be addressed later.

Programs such as FIRST allow the U.S. to engage countries while those decisions are still being made. They help governments build the capacity to evaluate competing technologies and financing arrangements while creating a pathway from initial interest to feasibility, engineering, financing, and ultimately investment.

Tesla has registered just 993 vehicles in India since it started deliveries there in September 2025, according to registration data compiled by Indian EV publication ElecTree .
But 294 of those came in September 2026 alone. That’s a record month for Tesla in India, and it comes right after the automaker cut prices and launched the six-seat Model Y L.
Tesla needed nine months to sell 428 cars
Tesla launched in India in July 2025 with a Model Y priced at roughly $70,000, almost twice what it cost in the US at the time. We said the price didn’t make sense.
The numbers agreed. Tesla registered 69 cars in September 2025, its first month of deliveries, and it didn’t beat that figure for the next eight months. It finished 2025 with 226 registrations and added only 202 more between January and May 2026, per ElecTree’s count. February was the low point at 29 cars.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
By January, Tesla was already discounting unsold Model Ys in India from its first batch of imports. In May, India’s Minister of Heavy Industries confirmed that Tesla won’t build a factory in India , which means every car it sells there keeps coming in as an import, with the duties that go with it.
A note on the “first year” math. The data covers 13 calendar months, September 2025 through September 2026. Count only the first 12 and Tesla is at 699 cars.
These are also registrations, not deliveries. Tesla doesn’t report sales by country, so registrations are the closest thing we get.
A price cut and the Model Y L changed the trend
Tesla made two moves this spring.
On April 22, it launched the Model Y L in India at ₹61.99 lakh (about $65,000), with deliveries starting in June. The longer six-seater came in cheaper than the five-seat Model Y Long Range, which was listed at ₹67.89 lakh (about $71,000) and has since been dropped from the lineup.
Then in late May, Tesla cut the entry-level Model Y by ₹9 lakh, from ₹59.89 lakh to ₹50.89 lakh. That’s a 15% cut, and it brings the starting price to about $53,000.
Registrations took off from there:
Month (2026) | Model Y L | Entry Model Y | Tesla total
June | 20 | 11 | 38
July | 85 | 26 | 116
August | 82 | 32 | 117
September | 238 | 56 | 294
Source: ElecTree registration data. Totals include the last Model Y Long Range units.
That’s 565 registrations in four months, more than the 428 Tesla managed in its first nine.
The Model Y L is doing most of the work. It has 425 registrations in four months, which is exactly what the entry-level Model Y has put up in 13. In September, the six-seater accounted for 81% of Tesla’s registrations in India.
The Model Y L launched in the US in July at $61,990 . So before taxes and fees, Indian buyers are paying within about $3,000 of the US price for an imported car, in a country with import duties of up to 110%. A year ago, Tesla was asking them to pay almost double.
It’s still a lot more than the roughly $47,000 the Model Y L launched at in China, where Tesla builds it.
Tesla has also added locations. It started with showrooms in Mumbai, Delhi, and Gurugram, and ElecTree reports that it has since opened in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, and Noida.
Tesla is still a rounding error in India
India registered 35,995 electric cars in September, up 98% from a year ago, according to Vahan registration data reported by Autocar Professional . Tata alone did 14,769. Tesla’s record month works out to 0.8% of India’s EV market.
Tesla looks better in the luxury segment. The same data has BMW at 502 electric cars in September, Tesla at 291, and Mercedes-Benz at 125.
So Tesla is now the second-biggest luxury EV brand in India with about 30% of the segment, up from 69 cars in the same month last year.
The comparison that stings is VinFast. The Vietnamese automaker registered its first cars in India the same month Tesla did. But it assembles them at a plant in Tamil Nadu, and it prices its SUVs between ₹18 lakh and ₹23 lakh (about $19,000 to $24,000).
VinFast registered 2,963 cars in India in September. That’s three times what Tesla has done in 13 months, in a single month.
Different price class, obviously. But it shows what building locally gets you in India.
Electrek’s Take
In January, we wrote that you can’t sell a $40,000 car for $70,000 and expect volume. Tesla tried it anyway and got 40 to 60 cars a month.
Then it cut the entry price by 15%, brought in a bigger car for less than the old top trim, and now it’s at almost 300 a month.
It must be a bit confusing for the Indian consumer.
It’s also hard to tell how much price changes affect volume compared to expansions in other cities.
Either way, for now, it looks like Tesla is not giving up on the Indian market despite the lackluster performance.

The founder of Omni Air International and former Sun Country Airlines CEO Jude Bricker have stepped in to buy the airline from private equity firm Stonepeak, which needed to quickly divest Omni Air to close a $2.53 billion parking meter concession from the city of Chicago over objections about Trump administration deportation flights.
Air Transport Services Group announced last Monday it has agreed to sell Omni Air, a passenger charter and outsourced airline provider, to OAI Holdings and focus on its cargo-related portfolio of airline, leasing, maintenance and logistics services companies. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter or early 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including approval by regulators. Financial terms were not disclosed.
No details about OAI Holdings or the investors behind the sale were provided. A news release said the new management team brings deep expertise in aviation. An ATSG representative declined to provide additional information. Stonepeak did not respond to repeated messages.
Stonepeak was under pressure from Chicago politicians to find an Omni Air buyer by Sept. 30 because of its contract with the Department of Homeland Security. The news release made no mention of the parking meter quid pro quo.
OAI Holdings was registered as a business in Nevada on Sept. 22, according to state filings reviewed by FreightWaves — six days before the sale was announced. The company has three officers, including Robert Coretz, who founded Omni Air in 1993 and was its chairman and CEO until 2018, when ATSG bought the company for $845 million. Cortez is currently on the advisory board at Omega Capital Management, and is affiliated with Amtra Capital Partners, an aircraft leasing and management firm — both based in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Omni Air is also headquartered in Tulsa.
The Cortez ownership group likely paid less for Omni Air than it originally sold for because it is a distressed asset.
Jude Bricker, who served as CEO of Sun Country Airlines until its sale to Allegiant Travel Co. in May and now sits on Allegiant’s board of directors, is also an officer. The third partner is Robert Waldo, the president of Kaiser-Francis Oil Co., an upstream oil and gas company owned by Kaiser Industries — and based in Tulsa.
OAI Holdings is a private company associated with Rob Coretz, according to the Airline Professionals Association, which represents pilots at Omni Air.
“In many ways, this sale to OAI Holdings appears to be a best-case scenario — a ‘return home’ for Omni and its pilots. In a phone call this morning, Omni President David Ray indicated that Mr. Coretz intends to rebuild, refleet, and grow Omni. And unlike other potential buyers, Mr. Coretz has the track record to make that a reality,” said David Pyers, a pilot and chairman of the Omni Pilots Executive Council, a unit of the Teamsters-affiliated Airline Professionals Association, in a message to members posted on the group’s website.
“For now, we view this as a positive development and are cautiously optimistic about what lies ahead,” he added.
Parking meters behind Omni exit
New York-based Stonepeak acquired ATSG last year when it was still publicly traded. Rather than an attempt to optimize the performance of a portfolio company, Stonepeak was motivated to unload Omni because of opposition to controversial deportation flights for Immigration and Customs Enforcement that threatened to derail a lucrative concession agreement with the city of Chicago, according to city council officials and local media .
Omni Air has conducted long-range deportation flights for many years, but the number of flights increased last year and included trips to remove immigrants to third countries where they had no ties.
More than a dozen members of the Chicago City Council declared they would not approve Stonepeak buying operating control of the city’s 36,000 parking meters for $2.53 billion under a 75-year lease unless it sold Omni Air. A Stonepeak official previously told the City Council that the company disagreed with the administration’s deportation policy and was actively trying to sell the company.
Omni Air International operates two Boeing 767-300 passenger jets for the New England Patriots, and the family of owner Robert Kraft, under a long-term contract. (Photo: ATSG)
In mid-September, a group of councillors struck a deal to allow the parking meter deal if Omni was sold. Stonepeak also agreed to pay the city $75 million once the sale closes and 5% of its net operating income from the parking meter business annually.
ATSG is the largest lessor of freighter aircraft in the world, with a fleet that mostly consists of Boeing 767-200 and -300 converted freighters sprinkled in with recent additions of Airbus A321 narrowbody and A330-300 medium-widebody jets. It is best known for owning cargo airlines ABX Air and Air Transport International, which provide the backbone for Amazon Air’s domestic air network and also support DHL Express. It also has a subsidiary that provides aircraft maintenance services.
Omni Air provides charter services for commercial and government customers, including the Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security and the New England Patriots football team. Omni also supplies aircraft and operating support to airlines through ACMI wet leasing and offers airline startup, route development and aircraft management services. Omni Air has 11 aircraft in its fleet: eight Boeing 767s and three 777-200 extended range jets.
Some, if not all of Omni Air’s airframes are owned by Cargo Aircraft Management, an ATSG subsidiary, which leases them to Omni. Nothing in the OAI Holdings sale announcement suggests that OAI Holdings is also purchasing the aircraft.
“This agreement marks an important step for ATSG as it reflects the advancement of our long-term strategy of investing in and building out our core air cargo and related aviation services businesses,” said CEO Greg Mays. “We have been assessing strategic options for Omni for some time given the significant opportunities in air cargo. This transaction allows us to focus our resources more fully on serving that market and related customers. We look forward to continuing to execute on our strategic vision, and are confident that OAI is the right next owner for Omni and their customers as they will benefit from OAI’s decades of proven aviation experience.”

ID 199691616 © Clare Jackson | Dreamstime.com
By Gavin van Marle
6 October 2026
With China’s Golden Week holiday under way and factories closed, supply chain planners’ attention has shifted to calculating shipping capacity out of Asia once Chinese workers return and container flows gear up again.
According to Drewry’s Cancelled Sailings tracker, 39 blanked sailings have been announced in the period from Week 41 (5–11 October) to Week 45 (2–8 November) across three deepsea east-west trades – the transpacific, transatlantic and Asia-Europe – 5% of the 710 scheduled voyages.
Half of the blanks will be on the transpacific, a third on Asia-Europe, and the remainder on the transatlantic.
However, while carrier capacity management has been blamed for the persistently strong transpacific container spot freight rates over he past two months, the scale of the blanks customers currently face – both in terms of voyages and overall slot capacity – is actually on the low side, in comparison with post-Covid norms.
“The data for blank sailings, shows that even though they still certainly do happen, the relative amount of capacity being blanked is actually quite low for the post-pandemic era,” analysts at Sea-Intelligence Consulting wrote this week.
“This is not to disparage shippers that have seen supply chains impacted by blanked sailings, but as an overall market status, reliability related to whether or not services are blanked is quite low presently.”
Its analysis of blanked sailings on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades, which takes January 2020 as its starting point, shows that on average around 10% of Asia-US west coast sailings are blanked in any given period, and “tactically, right now, the level of blank sailings is quite low”.
It found a similar number of blankings on the Asia-US east coast trade but added: “There is a slight hint of a downwards trend over the past two years, indicating a lower propensity for blank sailings amongst the carriers.”
Meanwhile, the Asia-North Europe trade is, as usual at the end of September, seeing its lowest level of blanking since the beginning of the pandemic, while the Asia-Mediterranean trade is also nearing historic lows.
For carriers, blankings are a demand response function, but one Europe forwarder told The Loadstar that “bookings for post-Golden Week seem steady so far”, while some pre-holiday shipments were expected to be rolled, “as we had no restrictions on bookings”.
It has left some forwarders scratching their heads, particularly as Asia-Europe carriers last began announcing FAK (freight all kinds) spot rate hikes in the second half of this month.
One said: “We’re still receiving reductions on FAK rates for the first half of October, which make the rate increases [around $1,000 per 40ft] I’ve seen for the second half, confusing. If carriers have enough cargo for a roll pool to increase rates, then why reduce rates for sailings in the first half?”
Drewry warned shippers that while most scheduled services were expected to sail this month, “the distribution of blank sailings across trades remains important”.
It added: “With demand patterns likely to shift after Golden Week, attention should remain on where carriers make further capacity adjustments, and how these changes affect space availability and schedules.
“This will be particularly relevant on Asia–Europe/Med, where the return of services to the Suez route is adding capacity to the trade, while comparatively limited cancellations on the transpacific could keep space availability firmer.”

Photo : © Dreamstime.com
By Alison Koo
6 October 2026
Teu-mile demand growth has regressed for the first time since January, reflecting a combination of blanked sailings by major carriers during China’s Golden Week, increased newbuild vessel deliveries, and more ships returning to the Suez Canal on Asia-Europe routes.
According to container shipping consultancy Linerlytica, several long-haul services have been cancelled in response to weaker Chinese export volumes during the week-long holiday that began on 1 October. The blanked sailings are concentrated on Asia-US East Coast and Asia-Europe trades.
Linerlytica said: “The return to the Suez route poses the biggest threat to carrier efforts to reverse the rate slide on the Asia-Europe route that have persisted for the past three months.
“All carriers are making a concerted rate push from the end of October, with MSC among the latest to announce new Asia-North Europe FAK (freight all kinds) rates from 19 October of $3,150 per teu and $4,500 per 40ft.”
Rates on that trade have fallen around 60% since July as the early peak-season momentum faded. On 2 October, the Shanghai Containerised Freight Index showed prices at $2,199 per teu, and $3,378 per 40ft.
Meanwhile, deliveries of new container vessels have accelerated after the usual summer lull. Nearly 200,000 teu of new capacity arrived last month, against no vessels demolished, adding further pressure to market capacity.
Linerlytica said its market barometer had now moved into negative territory, with shipping activity expected to remain subdued over the next two weeks. The faster-than-expected resumption of Suez Canal transits, however, remains the biggest obstacle to carrier efforts to support and increase freight rates.
ONE has become the latest major carrier to resume Suez Canal operations, following CMA CGM, Maersk, MSC, Hapag-Lloyd, and Cosco/OOCL. The 8,110 teu ONE Continuity , on the Japanese carrier’s South-east Asia-North Europe service, is scheduled to transit the Suez Canal later this month, after leaving Thailand’s Laem Chabang Port on 17 October.
Other members of the Premier Alliance have yet to follow, still citing security concerns. At the same time, cargo demand continues to weaken, adding further pressure to an already challenging container shipping market.

DoorDash has launched a retail returns service that lets customers pay $7.99 for a driver to pick up an eligible purchase at their door and take it back to the store. Dasher Returns is available in select cities, with a nationwide rollout expected in November.
What’s Related
The company announced the service Sept. 30 at its Dash Forward event. Customers do not need a box or shipping label, and DoorDash says pickup can happen in as little as 30 minutes. The retailer processes the return when the driver brings the item back, with the customer receiving a refund within days.
DoorDash also unveiled DoorDash Air, a drone delivery system that will begin pilot deliveries in Northern California. The returns service is already operating, while the drone announcement outlines an upcoming test with restaurant partners.

How the returns service works
Dasher Returns covers eligible retail orders and handles the trip from the customer’s home back to the store. DoorDash says it processes returns on the spot, allowing the item to go directly back on the shelf.
The service’s advertised speed comes with conditions. DoorDash says pickup times vary and are not guaranteed, refund timing can differ, and the $7.99 price is subject to change.
The retail announcement also details the scale of its new shopping partnerships. Macy’s products will be available through more than 350 stores, while Anthropologie will be available at more than 220 locations. The North Face, Vans, and Timberland together bring more than 350 stores.
Drone pilot starts with restaurant orders
DoorDash Air’s first partners include Chipotle, Popeyes, and Momo N Curry. DoorDash did not provide a specific start date for the Northern California pilot.
The company says it designed the system around actual order weights, sizes, and delivery distances. Its work includes packaging , loading equipment, and the handoff from restaurant kitchens to aircraft.
According to DoorDash, about 80% of typical restaurant orders are small and light enough for its aircraft to carry. Weather, flight range, and other conditions further narrow which orders can travel by air .
DoorDash says initial tests produced average restaurant-to-door delivery times of under five minutes, based on a limited sample. Its delivery software will consider the order’s contents, weight, distance, and traffic when choosing between a driver, a ground robot , or a drone.

The Kia EV3 starts at $29,890 in the US, and after a day of driving it around Vancouver Island, I think it’s the best-packaged affordable EV you can buy right now.
It comes with up to 321 miles of range, two battery sizes, and available all-wheel drive, which is more choice than anything else at this price. But there’s a catch: that $30,000 price tag climbs fast.
Kia brought me to Vancouver Island last week to test the EV3 as it launches in North America.
The Korean automaker took its time. The EV3 has been on sale overseas since 2024, and it quickly became one of the most popular EVs in Europe and won the 2025 World Car of the Year award before Kia finally decided to bring it here.

Now it’s here. US sales started in mid-August , and Kia told us it has about 1,300 units in dealer stock. According to the company, dealers love it because it’s bringing more shoppers into showrooms.
A Bolt EV with more options
Kia sees the EV3 as a competitor to the Chevy Bolt and the Nissan Leaf. Those are pretty much your only other choices if you want a new EV around $30,000 in the US.
The 2027 Bolt starts at $28,995 with 262 miles of range, and the 2026 Leaf starts at $29,990 with up to 303 miles. The EV3 lands right between them at $29,890 before a $1,495 destination fee .
By Kia’s count, there are nearly 80 EV models on sale in the US today, and only two of them were priced under $30,000 before the EV3 showed up. Not great.
The way I see it, the EV3 is really a Bolt EV that’s better packaged and comes with more options. You get to pick between two battery packs, front-wheel or all-wheel drive, and five trims, so you can end up with something closer to what you really want. Neither the Bolt nor the Leaf offers AWD.
The base Light FWD comes with a 58.3 kWh pack that’s good for 221 miles. For $34,990, the Wind FWD gets the 81.4 kWh pack and the full 321 miles. All-wheel drive adds a second motor for 261 hp and brings range down to 280 miles. At the top, the $45,890 GT makes 288 hp and gets to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds.
The EV3 also takes over from the Niro EV, which started at $39,700 with 253 miles of range. So Kia’s entry-level EV just got about $10,000 cheaper.
Small footprint, big battery
The EV3 is a boxy-looking compact SUV with Kia’s “tiger face” front end and the same design language as the EV6 and EV9.
Boxy usually means bad aero. But Kia focused on aero optimization and got the drag coefficient down to 0.275.
That’s a big reason why the base version gets impressive range out of a relatively small pack. And Kia still managed to fit a big 81.4 kWh pack into a vehicle that’s just 169.3 inches long. According to Kia, the new pack has 22% higher energy density than the one in the Niro EV.
The EV3 rides on a 400-volt version of the E-GMP platform, so don’t expect EV6 charging speeds. Peak rates are about 100 kW and 127 kW depending on the pack, but peak charge rates aren’t the whole story. At virtually any DC fast-charging station, you’ll be able to charge to 80% in roughly 30 minutes. Kia says that’s about 30% faster than the Niro EV.
It comes with a NACS port and Plug & Charge, which Kia says gives you access to more than 40,000 DC fast chargers.
The EV3’s NACS charge port on the front passenger-side fender
Inside, you get 26 cubic feet of cargo space behind the rear seats and about 56 cubic feet with them folded.
The EV3’s trunk with two backpacks
There’s also a 0.9 cubic-foot frunk. It’s small, but we often don’t see any frunk on a vehicle of this form factor, and Kia says it’s the only one in this segment. We appreciate Kia making the effort.
The Kia EV3’s 0.9 cubic-foot frunk
Kia says the EV3 has 99.7 cubic feet of passenger volume, which it claims is more than any of its direct competitors.
Front row
Rear legroom
When I sat in the back seat, I felt I had plenty of legroom with the front seat at a normal position, but when sitting straight, my head was within 3 inches of the ceiling (I’m 6ft tall).
The tech is what you’d expect from a more expensive EV: over-the-air updates, Apple CarPlay, and apps like YouTube and Netflix. Highway Driving Assist is standard on every trim, and a head-up display is available on the GT.
Dashboard
Front seats
Rear seats
One thing to watch: vehicle-to-load (V2L) isn’t available below the GT-Line. On the trims that have it, Kia includes the external adapter.
Driving the EV3
Kia sent us on a loop out of Victoria: north over the Malahat, west to Port Renfrew, and back along the coast. I drove the Wind FWD and the GT-Line AWD.
Kia’s drive route for the EV3 on Vancouver Island
The driving experience is impressive for an entry-level EV. The FWD version makes 201 hp and the AWD makes 261 hp. I never felt like I didn’t have enough power in either of them.
The EV3 also felt planted on the road, even on the tough logging roads around Vancouver Island. For a vehicle in that segment, I was pleasantly surprised by the driving experience.
Every EV3 gets four-wheel independent suspension, and Kia adds acoustic laminated glass on the windshield and front windows from the Wind trim up.
The Kia EV3 on Vancouver Island
Then there’s one-pedal driving, and it feels great. Kia’s new i-Pedal 3.0 gives you three regen levels, and you turn it on by pulling and holding the left paddle.
And Kia finally remembers your preferred setting between drives. If you’ve owned a Kia or Hyundai EV, you know how annoying it was to turn i-Pedal back on every time you got in the car.
The price goes up fast
My main concern is the “affordable” part.
It’s true that you can get an EV3 for $30,000. But the cheapest version I tested was still $41,000, and the GT-Line AWD starts at $43,490. The price goes up fast depending on the options, so be on the lookout for that.
Kia EV3 US trims and starting prices
The good news is that you don’t have to go that high. You can get the base version for $29,890, or the max range in a well-equipped Wind FWD for $34,990. That one looks like the sweet spot of the lineup.
Electrek’s Take
This is the affordable EV we have been waiting for.
To be fair, the bar isn’t high. The other choices around $30,000 are very limited, with just the Bolt EV and the Leaf. But the EV3 gives you more than either of them: two battery sizes, up to 321 miles of range, and AWD if you need it.
It’s a Bolt EV that’s better packaged, with enough optionality to get you closer to the vehicle you really want. And that’s from someone who likes the Bolt EV.
My worry is the pricing. If most of the EV3s on dealer lots look like the $41,000 one I drove, a lot of buyers will never see the “affordable EV” Kia is advertising. The $30,000 and $35,000 versions are the ones that matter.
But I think this can be a popular vehicle in North America like it already is in Europe. Kia sold 514 of them in the first full month, and I expect that number to go up from here as long as the Korean brand is making them available.
What do you think? Would you take the EV3 over the Bolt or the Leaf? Let us know in the comment section below.
